samples.question: This picture shows a network drawn on a white page. Every dark disc is a junction and every straight gray bar is a link joining the two junctions at its ends. Bars meet only at junctions, no bar crosses another bar, and no bar passes through a junction that is not one of its two ends. As drawn, the whole network hangs together: from any junction you can reach any other junction by travelling along bars. Exactly one junction is circled by a black ring, and exactly four bars touch that ringed junction. Now imagine rubbing out the ringed junction together with all four bars that touch it, and leaving every other junction and every other bar exactly as it is drawn. Two of the remaining junctions are in the same piece when you can still travel from one to the other along remaining bars; a remaining junction that is left with no bar at all is a piece on its own. How near two junctions look on the page does not matter, only what the bars still join. The rest of the network breaks into 1, 2 or 3 pieces. After the ringed junction and its four bars are rubbed out, how many separate pieces does the rest of the network fall into? Answer 1, 2, or 3.
